content: Avascular necrosis of the bone is a common and serious complication associated with sickle cell disease, and there is currently no standardized treatment for this condition. This review aimed to evaluate the effects of surgical interventions compared to other surgical or non-surgical treatments for avascular necrosis in individuals with sickle cell disease, focusing on both efficacy and safety. The search for relevant studies included a comprehensive review of electronic databases, handsearching of journals, and conference proceedings. Additional trials were identified through ongoing trial registries and reference lists of related papers. The most recent search was conducted on September 17, 2019. The inclusion criteria were randomized clinical trials that compared specific therapies for avascular necrosis in people with sickle cell disease. Only one trial, involving 46 participants, met the inclusion criteria. However, eight participants withdrew after randomization, primarily because they declined to continue in the study. As a result, data from 38 participants were analyzed at the end of the trial. The trial compared hip core decompression combined with physical therapy to physical therapy alone, with a mean follow-up period of three years. The results showed no significant clinical improvement in the group receiving hip core decompression and physical therapy compared to the group receiving physical therapy alone. The improvement scores were 18.1 points for the intervention group and 15.7 points for the control group, based on the original trial's scoring system. The evidence regarding major complications, such as hip pain, vaso-occlusive crises, and acute chest syndrome, was of very low quality. Specifically, the risk ratio for hip pain was 0.95 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.56 to 1.60), for vaso-occlusive crises was 1.14 (95% CI 0.72 to 1.80), and for acute chest syndrome was 1.06 (95% CI 0.44 to 2.56). The trial did not report data on mortality or quality of life. The authors concluded that there is no evidence to suggest that adding hip core decompression to physical therapy provides clinical improvement in individuals with sickle cell disease and avascular necrosis of the bone compared to physical therapy alone. However, this conclusion is based on a single trial with a high rate of participant withdrawal. Further randomized controlled trials are needed to better understand the role of hip core decompression in this condition. Future studies should prioritize endpoints that reflect participants' subjective experiences, such as quality of life and pain, as well as objective measures like mortality, survival, and hip longevity. Ensuring an adequate number of participants to achieve sufficient statistical power will be critical for the success of these trials.
